theme: Praise the LORD, all nations, the mission in two verses
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 117. It has only two verses. You met it earlier, in the unit on Luke. Read it now as the whole mission of Acts in miniature: the call to the nations and the reason.
settingTheScene: Psalm 117 is the shortest psalm and the shortest chapter in the Bible. Paul quotes it in Romans 15:11 to show that the Gentiles were always meant to glorify God. Placed here, in the middle of the first missionary journey, it is a summary of what Paul and Barnabas are doing: calling all nations to praise the LORD because of his steadfast love and faithfulness.
interpretation:
In two verses, the psalm gives the mission’s command and its motive. The command is to praise: “Praise the LORD, all nations! Extol him, all peoples!” The scope is every nation and every people. The motive is in verse 2: “For great is his steadfast love toward us, and the faithfulness of the LORD endures forever.”

Notice the logic. The nations are to praise because of God’s love “toward us,” toward Israel. The LORD’s covenant faithfulness to one people is the reason for the whole world to worship. In Acts, this is the heart of the mission. The God who kept his promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, to David, and to Israel in sending Jesus, is the God who is calling the nations. Paul preaches in Pisidian Antioch that God has fulfilled the promise made to the fathers. The Gentiles rejoice and glorify the word of the Lord. They are the “all peoples” called to praise.

Look at Paul’s use in Romans 15: Christ became a servant to the circumcised to show God’s truthfulness, in order to confirm the promises given to the patriarchs, and in order that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. Then Paul quotes a chain of passages, including this psalm: “Praise the Lord, all nations, and let all the peoples extol him.” The psalmist wrote this long before, and Paul says it is being fulfilled.

The psalm also gives the mission its fuel. Missionaries do not go out because of a program but because the LORD is worthy of praise from every people. Missions exists because worship doesn’t yet. The great goal is that all nations praise him, and the great ground is his steadfast love and faithfulness.

The psalm ends as it began, with “Praise the LORD!” We can do the same, grateful that his love is great toward us, and his faithfulness endures forever.
connection: Romans 15:8-12 quotes this psalm. Psalm 67, 96, 98, and 100 are similar missionary psalms. Genesis 12:3 and 22:18 are the Abrahamic promise. Isaiah 49:6 and 56:7 point to the nations coming. Acts 13:47-48 shows Gentiles glorifying the word of the Lord. Revelation 7:9-10 pictures the fulfillment.
application:
Recite the psalm aloud each morning this week. It takes ten seconds.

Name a nation or people group and pray the psalm over them.

Thank God that you belong to “all nations” because of his steadfast love.
prayerPrompts: Praise the LORD with all the nations.
Thank him for his great steadfast love toward us.
Pray for his word to reach someone far away.
